title: West Sikkim by shared jeep: routes, fares and timings
meta_description: How to travel West and South Sikkim by shared jeep and SNT bus: stands, morning timings, seat fares from Siliguri, Gangtok and Darjeeling, when to hire a car.
summary: Shared jeeps are the cheapest and most local way around West and South Sikkim. A seat from Siliguri to Pelling costs about ₹400–550 against ₹5,500–7,500 for a reserved car. The catch is timing: most jeeps leave in the morning, so plan each transfer day to start early.

sections.heading: How shared jeeps work here
paras: In the Sikkim hills the backbone of public transport is the shared jeep: a Mahindra Bolero, Tata Sumo or similar four-wheel-drive that runs a fixed route and leaves when it is full. Each vehicle carries about ten passengers, two or three beside the driver, four in the middle row and three or four at the back. Luggage goes on the roof under a tarpaulin, tied down by the driver or his helper.

Seats are sold at a counter or by the driver at a jeep stand. On busy routes you buy a numbered ticket and the jeep leaves at a set time; on quieter ones it waits until the seats fill. Fares are fixed by the local taxi associations and are usually printed or chalked up at the counter, so there is little bargaining. Sikkim Nationalised Transport (SNT) also runs buses on the main routes. They are slower, but cheaper and roomier.

For a budget traveller the saving is large. A reserved car from NJP to Pelling costs about ₹5,500–7,500; a shared jeep seat costs about ₹400–550, indicative for 2026. Even two people save around ₹4,500 on that one leg, which pays for two or three nights in a homestay.

sections.heading: Where the jeeps leave from
paras: Knowing the right stand saves an hour of confusion. Every town has one or two, usually near the market, and jeeps for different directions often leave from different corners of the same square. Ask your hotel the evening before and, in peak season, buy your ticket then.
list: Siliguri: jeep stands around the SNT terminus and the Tenzing Norgay bus terminus area on Hill Cart Road; from NJP station or Bagdogra airport take an auto or cab there first.
Gangtok: jeeps for Gyalshing, Ravangla and Namchi leave from the city's jeep stands; your hotel will know which stand serves the west that season.
Darjeeling: jeeps for Jorethang leave from the stands near Chowk Bazaar and the motor stand below the market.
Jorethang: the junction for West Sikkim, with jeeps to Gyalshing, Pelling, Soreng, Sombaria and Okhrey, Namchi and Siliguri.
Gyalshing: the hub of the west, with jeeps to Pelling, Yuksom, Tashiding, Khecheopalri, Uttarey and Dentam, Gangtok and Siliguri.
Legship, Ravangla and Namchi: smaller stands on the road between the west and the south.

sections.heading: Fares at a glance
paras: These are the seat fares we budget with for 2026. They are indicative: associations revise fares from time to time, and a front seat may cost a little more. Reserved car prices are for one car, one way. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Timing: the morning rule
paras: The single most important thing to know is that hill jeeps run in the morning. Long-distance jeeps from Siliguri, Gangtok and Darjeeling mostly leave between about 6.30 am and noon. The onward jeeps from junction towns such as Jorethang and Gyalshing thin out sharply after about 1 pm. Local runs like Gyalshing–Pelling keep going until late afternoon.

In practice this means two things. If your train reaches NJP or your flight lands at Bagdogra after about 11 am, you may not get a shared jeep all the way to Pelling the same day. Either stay a night in Siliguri and leave early, or take a jeep to Jorethang or Namchi and continue next morning. And on transfer days within the region, start by 8 am so a missed connection still leaves you a second chance.

Return jeeps from Yuksom, Tashiding and Uttarey towards Gyalshing usually leave early in the morning, often 6–8 am, because villagers ride them to the district headquarters for work and errands. Ask the evening before and be at the stand ten minutes early.

sections.heading: Riding well: seats, luggage and comfort
paras: The front seat beside the driver is the most comfortable and the best for people who get car-sick. On some routes you can ask for it when buying your ticket and pay a small extra. The middle row is the next best; the back row, facing sideways or backwards on some models, is the bumpiest.

Pack light. A 40–50 litre rucksack or a medium suitcase is fine on the roof, but wrap it in a rain cover or a plastic sheet even in the dry season, because dust and the odd shower get through the tarpaulin. Keep valuables, water, snacks and a warm layer with you inside. Drivers stop for tea and a toilet break on longer runs, usually at Melli, Jorethang or Legship.
list: Take motion-sickness tablets before, not during, the drive if you are prone to it.
Carry small notes; drivers rarely have change for ₹500.
Note the jeep number and the driver's phone number on long runs.
In the monsoon, ask whether the road is open before you buy a seat; landslides near Melli, Jorethang and Legship can close it for hours.

sections.heading: When a reserved car is worth it
paras: Shared jeeps get you between towns. They do not get you to the sights along the way. On the Pelling–Yuksom road, for example, the shared jeep runs straight through and you will not stop at Rimbi, Kanchenjunga Falls or Khecheopalri Lake. That is when a reserved car earns its price, especially if you split it.

Our rule of thumb: shared jeeps for long transfers, reserved cars for sightseeing days, and always try to share the car. Four travellers on a Pelling–Khecheopalri–Yuksom day pay about ₹600–700 each, not much more than the jeep seats would cost, and they see everything. Families with small children, older travellers and anyone with heavy bags will also find a reserved car worth the money on the Siliguri leg.

sections.heading: A week on shared jeeps: one way to do it
paras: Here is a loop we have used many times. Day one, an early jeep from Siliguri to Gyalshing and a local one up to Pelling. Day two, walk to Rabdentse, Pemayangtse and Sanga Choeling. Day three, down to Gyalshing for the midday jeep to Yuksom. Day four, Norbugang and Dubdi on foot. Day five, an early jeep to Tashiding, a morning at the monastery, then on to Legship and Ravangla. Day six, the Buddha Park and a short jeep ride to Namchi. Day seven, a morning jeep from Namchi back to Siliguri.

Seat fares for the whole loop come to roughly ₹1,600–2,300 per person, indicative for 2026. The same route by reserved car would cost a group ₹22,000–28,000. You trade some comfort and flexibility for that saving, and you gain conversations with the people who live here, which is often the part of the trip travellers remember longest.

sections.heading: Safety and solo travel
paras: Shared jeeps in Sikkim are a normal, everyday way to travel, used by students, workers and families, and they are generally safe for solo travellers including women. Drivers are experienced on these roads. Sit in the front or middle row if you prefer, keep your phone charged and share your route with someone. Foreign nationals must carry their Sikkim permit and passport, since checkposts at Melli, Rangpo and Jorethang may ask for them. Indian nationals should carry photo ID. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much is a shared jeep from NJP to Pelling
faqs.a: About ₹400–550 a seat from the Siliguri jeep stands to Gyalshing or Pelling, indicative for 2026, plus ₹50–80 if you change at Gyalshing. From NJP station take an auto to the stands near the SNT terminus first. Jeeps leave mostly in the morning. A reserved car costs ₹5,500–7,500. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What time do shared jeeps leave Siliguri for West Sikkim
faqs.a: Most leave between about 6.30 am and noon, with the busiest departures early in the morning. In peak season the later jeeps can sell out. If you arrive at NJP or Bagdogra after about 11 am, consider a night in Siliguri, a jeep only as far as Jorethang or Namchi, or a reserved car.

faqs.q: Is there an SNT bus from Siliguri to Pelling
faqs.a: Yes, Sikkim Nationalised Transport usually runs about one morning bus a day from its Siliguri terminus towards Pelling or Gyalshing, for around ₹300–400, indicative. It is slower than a jeep but roomier and cheaper. Buy the ticket a day ahead at the counter and confirm the departure time locally.

faqs.q: Can I go from Darjeeling to Pelling by shared jeep
faqs.a: Yes, in two legs. Take a morning shared jeep from Darjeeling to Jorethang, about ₹150–200 and 1.5–2 hours, then another from Jorethang to Gyalshing or Pelling for ₹150–250. Leave Darjeeling by 8 am because most Jorethang jeeps into West Sikkim go before about 1 pm.

faqs.q: How do I get from Pelling to Yuksom by shared jeep
faqs.a: Take a local shared jeep from Pelling down to Gyalshing, 25 minutes and ₹50–80, then a Yuksom jeep for ₹120–180, indicative. Yuksom jeeps usually leave Gyalshing around midday or early afternoon, so ask your hotel for that day's time. The jeep does not stop at the waterfalls or Khecheopalri on the way.

faqs.q: Can I book shared jeep seats in advance
faqs.a: On busy long-distance routes, yes: you can usually buy a ticket at the counter the evening before or early the same morning. Phone booking depends on the stand. Local routes are first come, first served. In October, Christmas week and May, book a day ahead for Siliguri, Gangtok and Gyalshing departures.

faqs.q: Are shared jeeps safe in the monsoon
faqs.a: Drivers are experienced and will not set off on a road they know is blocked, but monsoon roads do slip, and delays of hours are normal. Travel in the morning, ask whether the road is open before you buy a seat, and keep a spare day in your plan between June and September. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to hire a car for a group of four
faqs.a: For sightseeing days, often yes. Four people sharing a ₹2,500–3,500 car pay about the same as their jeep seats and see everything along the way. For long transfers such as Siliguri to Pelling, four jeep seats at about ₹2,000 total still beat a ₹5,500–7,500 car, but the car may be worth it with children or heavy bags.

faqs.q: Which is the best seat in a shared jeep
faqs.a: The front seat beside the driver: more legroom, a clear view and less motion sickness. You can sometimes request it when you buy the ticket and pay a little extra. The middle row comes next. Avoid the back row on long mountain runs if you get car-sick easily.
